You're implying that GPT-6 Sol can do better. That is not how LLMs work! They will write code, and then, in a separate invocation, find 100 problems with that code. You have to watch out for

2. Do you employ “shenanigans” to circumvent the checker? Bugs, unsafe operations. — Lean is a very strict checker as compilers go. As an ex- mathematician and ex- computer scientist who worked in programming language theory and computer algebra systems, I can assure you that we think about these problems deeply. In fact, outside of a few strongly normalizing toys, the first thing we do in PLT is drop completeness in favor of soundness. The article itself discusses this (the soundness issues that were addressed).

Although, now I'm charmed about the idea of a programming language -- possibly a Brainfuck descendent? -- that drops soundness for completeness.

I think the deeper problem - an I am reading Computational Reflections by Cantwell Smith and that might be colouring my view - is that fundamentally it comes down to the interpretation of what the code or the math says.

The very meaning of interpretation in computer science is at odds with the use in philosophy of language and that is symptomatic.

We're still fundamentally trying to advance Hilbert's program. It's like Göedel's work hasn't sunk in to our collective reasoning about reasoning. It just doesn't seem possible to build a self contained correct and truthful system of symbolic logic. Truth is in the relationship of the system with other systems.

Automating mathematics, like automating software engineering, or automating automation, are all self contradictory propositions. Anything of what we build only ever means anything in how it interacts with us. I mean, people will go round and round in this forum discussing semantics and the meta implication of these unceasing discussions never seems to hit home. Namely, that there is no universal, truthful, correct, system of symbolic logic. It seems in fact impossible to have one. But the results that indicate this impossibility are built with a system of symbolic logic and the validity therein is contingent on people's understanding and, like all symbolic logic systems (including the ones that states the limits to universal symbolic logic systems) they are bootstrapped from axioms one must chose at the start or by default and they can never be fully proved by the very system built atop them.

They are not talking about changing the theorem. The solution can arbitrarily chose to override or ignore certain things to make sure the theorem passes.

As in the infamous 2=1 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_fallacy#Division_...). We ignore that division by zero is undefined, and boom, we get a "proper" solution to the stated theorem.

That's what the article means by "how do we know for sure that somewhere in the millions of lines of code there is no hack which changes the meaning of the statement, changes the rules from just the axioms of mathematics".

As for the meaning of the statement, I don't know how it is easy in maths. But in code, I've had Claude try and contort the definition of "function accepts integers" to "anything that can look as an integer e.g. a string containing an integer is accepted" and twist the solution to that.

I don't understand this at all, as someone with a PhD in this area, and who uses lean quite a bit.

If 'Challenge.lean' states the theorem, the solution can't change the theorem. The only thing it can do is do a 'sorry', just skip proving some part, but that's printed out very clearly when it happens.

> Put another way — given a Challenge.lean file with only trusted code imported and the statement of a theorem, and a Solution.lean file with millions of lines of untrusted code imported and the proof of a theorem which looks identical, how do we know for sure that somewhere in the millions of lines of code there is no hack which changes the meaning of the statement, changes the rules from just the axioms of mathematics.

As someone with a PhD in mathematics, but no experience with Lean, I found this pretty surprising. Shouldn't there be some kind of encapsulation, which insulates the statement from the proof?

children.author: seanwilson
children.text:
> def FermatsLastTheorem : Prop := ∀ a b c n : ℕ, n ≥ 3 → a^n + b^n ≠ c^n

> This code imports Lean’s mathematics library Mathlib and then defines a mathematical statement which looks at first glance like it might be Fermat’s Last Theorem, but which actually is a trivially false statement because in Lean ℕ contains 0, so a = b = c = 0 and n = 3 gives a counterexample.

...

> The first question which one has to ask when judging a pdf which comes with some Lean code is: “what is the statement of the theorem in the Lean code, and does this correspond to the actual theorem statement in the pdf?” For a human Lean expert, this is typically (but not always) an easy question to answer. For example any Lean-competent human mathematician would be able to read the two lines of code above and observe that this was a mis-statement of Fermat’s Last Theorem.

To add to this, if the statement is wrong, the proof steps and other theorem statements that appear in the full proof are going to follow a path that goes with the wrong statement so there's further opportunities to see there's a mistake.

Often problems with the statement make it impossible to complete the proof, make it unexpectedly easy, or the proof takes a path that doesn't make sense with the correct statement in mind. In the above example, you would see from the easy counterexample found in the proof that the statement is wrong. The proofs aren't a black box.

It's like if your high-level requirements for a computer program (the theorem statement) had a mistake and someone implemented it (the proof). The implementation is going to follow a path that implements that mistake. So by looking at individual function definitions that were implemented, there's opportunities to spot the problem.
